context: Remark 4 While not explicitly stated, the noiseless realizability assumption in (Balcan et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2022) entails that the learner knows κt = 0 for all t ∈ [T ]. We introduce Assumption 3 because the excess risk measured within {f ◦ ĥ : f ∈ F} ⊂ F ◦ H can be misleading in estimating the excess risk with respect to the Bayes-optimal predictor, if only a limited number of examples are sampled for task t, as the risk of the best predictor in this class may itself be far from LPt (ft∗ ◦ h∗ ). Proposition 5 below highlights the hardness in a simple linear setting; its formal statement and proof (based on a reduction from (Kong and Valiant, 2018, Proposition 2)) are deferred to Appendix A.1. We conjecture that it may be impossible to design an algorithm whose sample complexity adapts to the quality of representation of ĥ without the knowledge of κt . That said, Assumption 3 can be relaxed to the knowledge of a sequence of upper bounds {νt } on the Bayes optimal risks. In this case, the objective for each task t would then be to learn a hypothesis with risk at most νt + ϵ. Algorithm 1 can be extended to work in this setting with an an analogous sample complexity guarantee to our main result (Theorem 14 below).
